body:
Why did a new approach to nationalism emerge?

The Indian National Congress, established in 1885, initially relied mainly on constitutional methods to secure political and administrative reforms. Its early leaders, commonly called Moderates, believed that petitions, resolutions, public meetings and reasoned criticism could persuade the British government to accept Indian demands.

By the 1890s, a growing group of nationalists questioned whether these methods were sufficient. They argued that British rule depended on India's political and economic subordination and that meaningful self-government required Indians to organise and act for themselves. These leaders became known as Extremists, Radicals or Assertive Nationalists.

The term Extremist in this historical context describes a more assertive political approach. It does not mean that every leader supported violence. Many advocated organised public protest, economic self-reliance and the withdrawal of cooperation from colonial institutions.

Moderates and Extremists: the central distinction

AspectModeratesExtremists
Political approachSeek reforms through constitutional demands and persuasion.Build pressure through assertive public action and self-reliance.
Main methodsPetitions, resolutions, speeches and representations.Boycott, swadeshi, national education and mass mobilisation.
Role of the peopleDevelop informed public opinion to influence government.Encourage wider participation and organised resistance.
Attitude to British intentionsPlace greater hope in obtaining concessions through appeals.Argue that Indians must rely primarily on their own strength.

This distinction should not be made absolute. Moderates also criticised colonial economic policies and organised public meetings. Both groups belonged to the wider struggle against colonial rule. Their main differences concerned the speed, scope and methods of political action.

The idea of swaraj

Swaraj

Swaraj means self-rule or self-government. Assertive nationalists argued that Indians should exercise political authority over their own affairs rather than depend on concessions granted by colonial rulers.

Bal Gangadhar Tilak expressed the demand for freedom through the slogan, Freedom is my birthright and I shall have it! He also used the Marathi newspaper Kesari to criticise British rule and spread nationalist ideas.

The three leaders remembered as Lal–Bal–Pal

  • Lal: Lala Lajpat Rai was a prominent nationalist leader from Punjab.
  • Bal: Bal Gangadhar Tilak was associated with Maharashtra.
  • Pal: Bipin Chandra Pal was a prominent nationalist voice from Bengal.

These leaders were not members of a single formal office or committee called Lal–Bal–Pal. The expression identifies 3 influential figures associated with the assertive nationalist current in different regions.

Opposition to the partition of Bengal in 1905 gave these ideas a powerful opportunity for public action. Economic boycott, swadeshi production and national education now became closely connected with political protest.

Prelims focus

  • The early Congress mainly followed constitutional and persuasive methods associated with the Moderates.
  • Assertive nationalism grew in influence during the 1890s and early 1900s.
  • Lal–Bal–Pal refers to Lala Lajpat Rai, Bal Gangadhar Tilak and Bipin Chandra Pal.
  • Tilak edited the Marathi newspaper Kesari.
  • Trap: Extremist nationalism and secret revolutionary violence were not identical movements.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – III, Class 8, 2020–21 edition, chapter 9, The Making of the National Movement: 1870s–1947, printed pp. 111–114.]

pictures.caption: Public participation became increasingly important to the national movement in the early 1900s.

title: The Rise of Extremist Nationalism: Ideas, Leaders and Methods

body:
The province before partition

At the beginning of the 20th century, the Bengal Presidency covered a much larger administrative territory than present-day West Bengal. It included Bengal, Bihar and Orissa. British officials argued that administering such an extensive province from Calcutta was difficult.

Lord Curzon, the Viceroy of India, proceeded with the partition of Bengal in 1905. The Government of India issued a resolution concerning the territorial reorganisation on 19 July 1905. The partition took effect on 16 October 1905.

How was Bengal divided?

The reorganisation created a new province called Eastern Bengal and Assam, with its capital at Dacca, now Dhaka. The remaining Bengal province included western Bengal together with Bihar and Orissa, with Calcutta as its administrative centre.

Administrative justification and political opposition

The colonial government presented the partition as an administrative measure intended to improve governance. Nationalists, however, argued that the selected boundaries had an important political purpose: to weaken organised opposition to British rule and divide Bengali-speaking people.

The existing nationalist movement was particularly active in Bengal. By separating eastern and western areas, the government could reduce the political influence of organisations centred in Calcutta. Critics therefore described the measure as an example of divide-and-rule, a policy that seeks to weaken opposition by creating or exploiting divisions among groups.

Distinguish the claim from the criticism

British justification: Bengal was too large for convenient administration. Nationalist criticism: the boundaries also served the political purpose of weakening Bengali nationalism. These are different explanations of the same decision.

How did the anti-partition movement begin?

Opposition developed even before the partition came into force. At a major meeting in Calcutta Town Hall on 7 August 1905, protesters endorsed the boycott of British goods. The agitation brought together leaders from different tendencies within the Congress, although disagreements later emerged over how widely boycott should be applied.

On 16 October 1905, the day the partition became effective, many opponents observed mourning and public demonstrations. Rabindranath Tagore encouraged the tying of rakhi as a symbol of unity among people divided by the new administrative boundary.

The protest was not simply about government offices or provincial boundaries. It expressed the belief that colonial authorities should not be able to weaken the political and cultural unity of the people without facing organised opposition.

Annulment in 1911 and reorganisation in 1912

The British government announced the annulment of the 1905 partition in 1911. The subsequent administrative changes took effect in 1912. Eastern and western Bengal were reunited, while Assam again became a separate province and Bihar and Orissa were organised into another province.

Thus, annulment did not restore every administrative boundary that had existed before 1905. It ended the controversial division of Bengali territory while introducing a different provincial arrangement.

Prelims focus

  • Viceroy associated with the 1905 partition: Lord Curzon.
  • Government resolution concerning the partition: 19 July 1905.
  • Anti-partition boycott resolution at Calcutta Town Hall: 7 August 1905.
  • Partition implemented: 16 October 1905.
  • Annulment announced: 1911; administrative reorganisation followed in 1912.
  • Trap: The 1911 annulment did not restore the entire pre-1905 provincial arrangement unchanged.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – III, Class 8, chapter 9, printed pp. 113–114; Government of India, Resolution on the Partition of Bengal, 19 July 1905, reproduced in Prithwis Chandra Ray, The Case Against the Break-up of Bengal, Appendix A; Government of India, Report of the States Reorganisation Commission, 1955, printed p. 3, paragraphs 22–23; Rabindra Tirtha, Rabindranath Tagore chronology, 1905 entries, consulted 21 November 2026.]

pictures.alt: Bengal's provincial administration before 1905, its division in 1905, annulment in 1911, and the new provincial arrangement in 1912.
pictures.caption: The partition changed provincial administration; it was not the partition of India in 1947.

title: Partition of Bengal in 1905: British Decision and Nationalist Opposition

body:
How did the Swadeshi Movement develop?

The Swadeshi Movement emerged as a major response to the partition of Bengal in 1905. It sought to oppose the colonial decision while strengthening Indians' ability to meet their needs through their own products, institutions and efforts.

The movement was strongest in Bengal, but its ideas spread to other regions. In parts of coastal Andhra, the agitation was also known as the Vandemataram Movement.

Swadeshi and boycott are related but distinct

Two connected methods

Swadeshi means encouraging the use and production of goods made within one's own country. Boycott means deliberately refusing to buy, use or support particular goods or institutions as an act of protest.

During the anti-partition agitation, refusing foreign cloth was an act of boycott. Purchasing Indian-made cloth instead was an act of swadeshi. The first method reduced support for imported goods; the second attempted to strengthen indigenous production.

They were often practised together, but neither term is simply another name for the other. A person could support Indian enterprise through swadeshi even when not participating in a public boycott demonstration.

How did people participate?

  • Boycott of foreign goods: Protesters discouraged the purchase of British-made cloth and other imported products.
  • Public demonstrations: Meetings, processions and organised protests spread the demand to reverse Bengal's partition.
  • Picketing: Protesters gathered outside shops selling foreign goods to persuade customers not to enter or purchase them.
  • Public rejection of foreign cloth: Some demonstrators participated in the symbolic burning of imported textiles.
  • Support for Indian enterprise: Nationalists encouraged locally owned industries and the manufacture of everyday goods.
  • National education: Supporters promoted educational institutions operating under Indian direction rather than depending entirely on colonial control.

These methods connected political resistance with ordinary economic decisions. Buying cloth, selecting a school or supporting a local manufacturer could become a way to express opposition to British rule.

Why did economic self-reliance matter?

British manufactured textiles had gained a large share of Indian markets during the colonial period. Indian producers faced competition from machine-made imported goods, many of which could be sold cheaply. Swadeshi supporters believed that dependence on foreign manufactures weakened India's economic position.

They therefore encouraged the creation and expansion of Indian enterprises. The campaign also increased nationalist interest in protecting domestic manufacturing. Its purpose was both economic, by supporting indigenous production, and political, by challenging colonial authority through collective action.

Participation and practical limitations

Students, women, traders and sections of the educated public participated in different ways. Nationalist songs and local meetings helped take the movement beyond formal Congress proceedings. The forms and scale of participation varied across regions and social groups.

There were important economic limits. Indian-made alternatives were not always available at prices that poorer consumers could afford. Cheap imported manufactured goods remained difficult for local producers to compete against. For some families, choosing a more expensive swadeshi product involved a genuine financial sacrifice.

The movement therefore encouraged wider participation but did not involve every social group equally. It also did not immediately remove India's dependence on British goods.

Do not confuse an aim with an achieved result

Swadeshi aimed to strengthen indigenous industry and economic independence. This does not mean that the boycott eliminated imports or that all Indian consumers could afford domestically produced alternatives.

Prelims focus

  • The Swadeshi Movement gained momentum after the partition of Bengal in 1905.
  • Swadeshi encouraged Indian goods and enterprises; boycott rejected foreign goods or selected institutions.
  • Important methods included picketing, public demonstrations and support for national education.
  • In parts of coastal Andhra, the movement was called the Vandemataram Movement.
  • Trap: Swadeshi was not limited to burning foreign cloth; it also promoted constructive economic and educational activity.

[NCERT, Our Pasts – III, Class 8, chapter 9, printed pp. 113–114; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World – I, Class 9, 2018–19 edition, chapter Clothing: A Social History, section 5.1, printed pp. 172–173; NCERT, India and the Contemporary World – II, Class 10, chapter The Age of Industrialisation, section 5, printed pp. 121–122.]

pictures.alt: Shoppers examine Indian-woven cloth in a Bengali market as residents peacefully boycott imported cloth during the 1905 Swadeshi agitation.
pictures.caption: Choosing Indian-made cloth became an everyday expression of political resistance.

pictures.alt: Boycott and swadeshi shared economic aims in 1905, but higher costs and limited availability of Indian goods made participation unequal.
pictures.caption: Boycott and swadeshi worked together, although the availability and cost of Indian goods could limit participation.

title: Swadeshi and Boycott: Meaning, Methods and Public Participation
